title: Kant III: Enlightenment, Peace and the Sublime
subtitle: Dare to think for yourself — and then look up at the storm
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Kant's definition of enlightenment and the motto “sapere aude”.
By the end you will be able to distinguish the public and private uses of reason.
By the end you will be able to summarize the main proposals of *Toward Perpetual Peace* and connect them to modern institutions.
By the end you will be able to describe Kant's account of the beautiful and the sublime in the *Critique of the Power of Judgment*.
By the end you will be able to identify tensions and blind spots in Kant's political thought.
hook:
In December 1784 a Berlin magazine, the *Berlinische Monatsschrift*, printed an essay by a sixty-year-old professor from Königsberg. A year earlier, a clergyman writing in the same magazine had dropped a provocative question in a footnote: everyone keeps talking about enlightenment, but what *is* it? Several writers answered, including the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. But it is Kant's answer that is still quoted on posters, university crests and coffee mugs: *Sapere aude!* Have the courage to use your own understanding.

This lesson shows a different side of Kant from the austere theorist of the last two days. Here he is a public intellectual writing short, punchy essays about freedom of thought, a political visionary sketching a world federation to end war, and a philosopher of art trying to explain why a sunset strikes us as beautiful and why a thunderstorm over the ocean fills us with an exhilarating kind of fear. Together, these writings show how Kant's critical philosophy reaches into public life, international politics and our experience of nature.

sections.heading: What Is Enlightenment?
sections.body:
Kant's essay, *An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?* (1784), opens with one of the most famous definitions in philosophy:

> Enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-incurred immaturity.

Every word matters. **Immaturity** (the German *Unmündigkeit* also suggests the legal status of a minor who needs a guardian) means being unable to use your own understanding without direction from someone else. It is **self-incurred** when the cause is not a lack of intelligence, but a lack of resolve and courage. So the motto of enlightenment is **sapere aude**, a Latin phrase borrowed from the Roman poet Horace, which literally means “dare to be wise” and which Kant glosses as: have courage to use your own understanding.

Why do people stay immature? Kant's answer is uncomfortably honest: laziness and cowardice. It is *so comfortable* to be a minor. If I have a book that understands for me, a pastor who has a conscience for me, a doctor who decides my diet for me, then I do not need to think at all. And the guardians who have kindly taken charge of us make sure we find the step to maturity frightening, like domestic animals that are shown the dangers of walking without the harness.

This is a picture of enlightenment not as a body of correct opinions but as an *activity* and an *attitude*. It is not enough to swap old authorities for new ones — to believe the scientists instead of the priests simply because they are now in charge. Enlightenment means thinking for yourself. Notice how this echoes the ideal of autonomy from yesterday (Day 56): just as the moral agent gives herself the moral law, the enlightened thinker refuses to hand over her judgment to someone else.

Kant also thought enlightenment is hard for an individual alone and much easier for a public. Once a few independent thinkers exist, they spread a spirit of rational self-respect. But he warned that a revolution might topple a tyrant without producing a real reform in ways of thinking; new prejudices would simply replace the old ones as a leash for the unthinking masses. Enlightenment must come slowly.

sections.heading: Public Reason, Private Duty, and Frederick's Bargain
sections.body:
How can a society become enlightened? Kant's answer is one thing only: freedom to make **public use of one's reason** in all matters. But he draws a distinction that can confuse modern readers, because he uses “public” and “private” in an unexpected way.

The **public use of reason** is the use a person makes of it as a scholar addressing the whole reading public — writing books, articles, letters to the world. The **private use of reason** is the use a person makes of it in a particular post or office entrusted to them. Kant gives three examples:

- An army officer given an order should not argue about it on duty; he must obey. But as a scholar he may publicly criticize military policy.
- A citizen cannot refuse to pay taxes. But he may publish arguments that the taxes are unjust.
- A clergyman must teach his congregation according to the church's creed, because that is the job he accepted. But as a scholar he may publish his doubts and suggestions for reform to the world.

So Kant's formula is: in your role, comply; in the public sphere, argue freely. He praises the king of Prussia, Frederick the Great, for allowing this, and quotes the ruler's attitude: argue as much as you want and about whatever you want, but obey!

This is a fascinating and slightly uneasy bargain. On one reading it is a clever strategy: a reforming philosopher reassures an absolute monarch that free debate will not cause disorder, while slipping in the claim that rulers gain by listening. On another reading it is too timid, accepting obedience in exchange for permission to talk. Kant himself noticed a paradox: a large degree of civil freedom seems good for the people's freedom of spirit, yet sets it limits that cannot be overstepped. He also said clearly that we do not yet live in an *enlightened* age, but in an age of *enlightenment* — a process still under way.

The bargain was fragile. After Frederick died in 1786, his successor's government tightened censorship. In 1794 Kant received a royal rebuke for his writings on religion and promised, as the king's loyal subject, not to write on the topic again. When the king died in 1797, Kant considered himself released from the promise. Even the great defender of public reason had to bend before power.

sections.heading: Toward Perpetual Peace
sections.body:
In 1795, Prussia signed the Peace of Basel with revolutionary France. Kant, now in his seventies, responded with a short book called *Toward Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch*. It opens with a joke. A Dutch innkeeper, Kant says, had a sign showing a graveyard with the words “To Perpetual Peace”. Was the satire aimed at humanity in general, at rulers who never tire of war, or at philosophers who dream sweet dreams? Kant leaves the question open and then sets out his dream anyway.

The book is written like a mock peace treaty. First come **preliminary articles**, conditions to reduce the causes of war. Among them: no peace treaty should secretly reserve the material for a future war; standing armies should in time be abolished; no state should forcibly interfere in the constitution and government of another; and no state at war should use methods, such as assassination or incitement to treason, that would make mutual trust impossible in a future peace.

Then come the three **definitive articles**:

1. The civil constitution of every state should be **republican**. By this Kant means a state with the rule of law, separation of the legislative and executive powers, and citizens who are free and equal under the law. His reasoning: if citizens must consent to war, they will think hard before bringing its miseries upon themselves, whereas a monarch can declare war as casually as he plans a hunting party.
2. The law of nations should be founded on a **federation of free states**. Not a single world government, which Kant feared would become a soulless despotism, but a voluntary and expanding league of peace.
3. **Cosmopolitan right** should be limited to conditions of universal hospitality: a stranger has the right not to be treated with hostility on arrival in another land, though not a right to settle there. Kant used this point to attack European colonialism directly, condemning the injustice European powers showed when they visited foreign lands and peoples, which for them amounted to conquering them.

Kant was not naïve about human nature. He wrote that the problem of setting up a state can be solved even for a nation of devils, so long as they have understanding: well-designed institutions can make selfish people behave as if they were good. Peace is not a gift of saints but an achievement of good design, pushed along by commerce and by the sheer exhaustion of war.

sections.heading: The Third Critique: What Makes Something Beautiful?
sections.body:
In 1790 Kant published the third and final *Critique*, the *Critique of the Power of Judgment*. It tries to connect the two worlds of the earlier *Critiques*: nature, governed by causal law (Day 55), and freedom, governed by moral law (Day 56). The bridge, Kant thought, lies in our experience of purpose and design, whether in beautiful things or in living organisms. Today we focus on the first half, on beauty, which became a founding text of modern **aesthetics**, the philosophy of art and beauty.

Kant begins by separating different kinds of pleasure. The **agreeable** is what pleases the senses: I like this coffee, you prefer tea, and there is no point arguing. The *good* pleases through a concept of its purpose: a knife is good if it cuts well. But a **judgment of taste** — “this rose is beautiful” — is strangely in between. Kant offers four marks:

- It is **disinterested**. When I find a palace beautiful, I am not thinking about whether I want to own it or live in it. The pleasure does not depend on any desire for the object's existence.
- It claims **universal** agreement, yet without a concept. When I say the rose is beautiful, I speak as if everyone *ought* to agree, unlike “I like coffee”. Yet I cannot prove it with a rule or argument; there is no formula for beauty.
- It involves **purposiveness without purpose**. A beautiful thing seems as if designed to be grasped by our minds, its form fitting our faculties perfectly, yet it serves no particular function we can name.
- It is **necessary**, in the sense that we feel others should share our response, because it rests on a *common sense* that all human beings share.

Why can we demand agreement without proof? Kant's explanation is that beauty sets our imagination and understanding into a **free play**, a harmonious activity in which the mind enjoys its own capacity to make sense of things without being tied down to any particular concept. Because all humans share these faculties, we may expect others to feel the same.

Kant also suggests that beauty is a **symbol of morality**. In both cases we rise above mere desire toward something universal. Learning to love something without wanting to possess it is a kind of training for the moral life.

sections.heading: The Sublime: Delight in Terror
sections.body:
Beauty is not the only aesthetic experience. Stand on a cliff in a storm, watch the ocean roar, gaze at the Milky Way, and you feel something quite different: awe mixed with fear, a sense of your own smallness that is somehow thrilling. The eighteenth century called this the **sublime**. The Irish thinker Edmund Burke had analyzed it in *A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful* (1757), linking it to terror experienced from a safe distance. Kant had read Burke and also written an early book on the topic in 1764, but in the third *Critique* he gave the sublime a strikingly original twist.

Kant distinguishes two kinds:

- The **mathematical sublime** arises from sheer size. Faced with the vastness of the starry sky or the Alps, our imagination tries to take in the whole and fails. Yet reason can still *think* the idea of infinity, which no sense image could ever contain.
- The **dynamical sublime** arises from overwhelming power: hurricanes, volcanoes, waterfalls. Physically, we are helpless before them. Yet, watching from safety, we discover in ourselves a different kind of strength: a moral and rational self that nature cannot crush.

So for Kant, the sublime is not really in nature at all. Nature is the occasion; the sublimity belongs to our own minds. The feeling begins with pain (my senses are overwhelmed) and turns into pleasure (I discover that my reason and freedom transcend anything nature can throw at me). This is why the sublime connects so naturally to Kant's ethics. The same faculty that makes us feel awe before the moral law in us makes us feel awe before the storm.

Kant's ideas fed directly into Romantic painting and poetry — think of Caspar David Friedrich's lone wanderer gazing over a sea of fog — and into the philosophy of Schopenhauer (Day 60), who made aesthetic contemplation an escape from the miseries of desire.

A word of honesty: Kant's 1764 book on the beautiful and sublime also contains crude and offensive generalizations about women and non-European peoples, and similar remarks appear in his anthropology lectures. The thinker who demanded respect for every rational being did not consistently extend it. Scholars debate whether his views changed — *Perpetual Peace*, with its attack on colonial conquest, suggests at least some development — but the tension is real, and it is one reason later thinkers (Day 86) asked whose reason the Enlightenment really meant.

keyQuote.text: Enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-incurred immaturity.
keyQuote.source: Immanuel Kant, An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment? (1784)

modernConnection.title: A Book That Understands for Me: Thinking in the Age of AI
modernConnection.body:
Reread Kant's list of comfortable guardians: a book that understands for me, a pastor who has a conscience for me, a doctor who decides my diet for me. Now update it. A search engine that answers for me. A recommendation algorithm that chooses my music, films and news. A fitness app that decides my diet. An AI chatbot that writes my essay, summarizes the article I never read, and tells me what to think about it. Kant's 1784 diagnosis of “self-incurred immaturity” reads like a commentary on our relationship to technology.

The point is not that these tools are bad. Kant himself relied on books, doctors and scholars; nobody can check everything personally. The question is whether we use them as *aids* to our own judgment or as *substitutes* for it. Researchers have studied cognitive offloading, for example how relying on GPS can reduce people's engagement with spatial memory, and teachers worry that easy AI answers can short-circuit the struggle in which real understanding forms. Kant's warning that the guardians make independence look frightening also fits: it can feel risky to trust your own reading of a situation when an authoritative-sounding system has already given an answer.

Kant's public use of reason also has a modern echo. Social media promised a global public sphere, where anyone could address the world as a “scholar”. In some ways it delivered: censorship is harder, and ordinary people can challenge the powerful. But the platform rewards outrage and speed, not the patient, reasoned argument Kant had in mind. We will see the German philosopher Jürgen Habermas develop this idea of a public sphere on Day 80.

Where does the comparison break down? Kant's guardians were people with interests and responsibilities, and his solution was free public debate among humans. Today some of our guardians are systems whose reasoning even their designers cannot fully explain. *Sapere aude* still applies — but daring to think for yourself may now require understanding how your tools think, too.

vocabulary.definition: For Kant, humanity's emergence from self-incurred immaturity; the process of learning to use one's own understanding without another's guidance.
vocabulary.example: For Kant, enlightenment was less a set of correct beliefs than a habit of thinking for yourself.

vocabulary.definition: Latin phrase from Horace, “dare to be wise”, which Kant made the motto of the Enlightenment: have courage to use your own understanding.
vocabulary.example: She wrote “sapere aude” on her notebook as a reminder to check the sources herself.

vocabulary.definition: In Kant's sense, the use of reason as a scholar addressing the whole reading public, which must be free.
vocabulary.example: The officer obeyed the order on duty, then made public use of reason by publishing a critique of the policy.

vocabulary.definition: Kant's term for a state based on the rule of law, separation of powers, and free and equal citizens, which he believed would be slow to go to war.
vocabulary.example: Kant argued that a republican constitution makes war harder, since citizens must bear its costs.

vocabulary.definition: Kant's principle that strangers have a right to hospitality — not to be treated with hostility on arrival — though not a right to settle.
vocabulary.example: Kant used cosmopolitan right to condemn European conquest disguised as visiting.

vocabulary.definition: Pleasure in an object's form that does not depend on any desire to possess or use it; for Kant, the mark of a judgment of beauty.
vocabulary.example: Admiring a stranger's garden without wanting it for yourself is a case of disinterested pleasure.

vocabulary.definition: Kant's phrase for the way a beautiful thing seems designed to fit our minds, though it serves no particular function.
vocabulary.example: A seashell's spiral shows purposiveness without purpose: it seems perfectly arranged for our gaze, yet it wasn't made for us.

vocabulary.definition: The feeling of awe mixed with fear before something overwhelmingly vast or powerful, which for Kant reveals the superiority of our reason over nature.
vocabulary.example: Watching lightning over the ocean from a safe harbor, he felt the sublime.

thinkingExercise.title: An Audit of Your Guardians
thinkingExercise.prompt: Kant says we stay immature out of laziness and fear, letting guardians think for us. Spend 10–15 minutes identifying your own guardians and deciding which ones you trust wisely and which you trust lazily.
steps: List five sources you rely on to make up your mind (a news app, a friend, a doctor, a search engine, an AI tool, a religious or political authority).
For each, ask: when did I last disagree with it or check it independently? Mark it “aid” if you use it to support your judgment and “substitute” if you simply accept what it says.
Pick one “substitute” and imagine what it would take to make your own judgment on that topic. What would you need to learn, and what are you afraid of?
Finally, recall a moment when you felt the sublime or the beautiful in nature. Did it make you feel small, free, or both? Write a few sentences comparing your experience with Kant's account.

summary: Kant defined enlightenment as emergence from self-incurred immaturity, with the motto sapere aude: have courage to use your own understanding.
He demanded freedom for the public use of reason (as a scholar addressing the world) while accepting limits on the private use of reason in one's office.
Toward Perpetual Peace proposed republican constitutions, a federation of free states and cosmopolitan hospitality, and condemned colonial conquest.
In the Critique of the Power of Judgment, beauty is disinterested, claims universal agreement without a concept, and shows purposiveness without purpose.

The sublime, mathematical or dynamical, begins in being overwhelmed and ends in awareness of our own rational and moral power; Kant's universalism coexisted with prejudiced views that scholars still debate.

quiz.question: According to Kant, why is immaturity “self-incurred”?
options: Because it results from a lack of education provided by the state
Because its cause is a lack of resolve and courage, not a lack of understanding
Because children are naturally immature
Because churches force people to obey
quiz.explanation: Kant blames laziness and cowardice: people have the ability to think but lack the courage to use it without guidance.

quiz.question: In Kant's terms, which of the following is a *public* use of reason?
options: A soldier arguing with his commanding officer during a battle
A tax official refusing to collect a tax
A pastor preaching the official creed to his congregation
A pastor publishing a book criticizing his church's creed
quiz.explanation: Public use means addressing the reading public as a scholar. The pastor's sermon is a private use, tied to his office.

quiz.question: Kant claimed that his own time was already a fully enlightened age.
quiz.explanation: Kant said it was an age of enlightenment, not an enlightened age: the process was under way but far from complete.

quiz.question: Why did Kant believe a republican constitution would make war less likely?
options: Because citizens who must consent to war and bear its costs would hesitate to start one
Because republics cannot afford armies
Because republics are ruled by philosophers
Because a world government would forbid war
quiz.explanation: Kant argued that those who suffer war's miseries will think carefully before agreeing to it, unlike a monarch who risks little.

quiz.question: What kind of international order did Kant propose in Toward Perpetual Peace?
options: A single world government with one army
A balance of power maintained by alliances
A voluntary federation of free states
An empire led by the most enlightened nation
quiz.explanation: Kant feared a world state would become a soulless despotism, so he proposed an expanding league of free states.

quiz.question: Kant used his principle of cosmopolitan right to criticize European colonial conquest.
quiz.explanation: In Perpetual Peace he condemned the injustice of European powers, for whom visiting foreign lands amounted to conquering them.

quiz.question: What does Kant mean when he says a judgment of beauty is “disinterested”?
options: The person making it is bored by the object.
The pleasure does not depend on wanting to possess or use the object.
Everyone agrees about it.
It is based on a clear concept of the object's purpose.
quiz.explanation: Disinterested pleasure is independent of desire for the object's existence. It does not mean uninterested, and universal agreement is a separate mark.

quiz.question: Someone says “I like pineapple on pizza” and someone else says “This sonata is beautiful.” How would Kant distinguish these judgments?
options: Both are equally subjective, with no claim on anyone else.
Both can be proved by rules of taste.
The first is about the beautiful; the second is about the agreeable.
The first is about the agreeable and claims no agreement; the second claims everyone ought to agree, though it cannot be proved.
quiz.explanation: Judgments of the agreeable are private preferences. Judgments of beauty claim universal validity without resting on any concept or proof.

quiz.question: For Kant, where does sublimity ultimately lie?
options: In our own minds, which discover a rational power superior to nature
In large mountains and oceans themselves
In works of art that imitate nature
In God's design of the world
quiz.explanation: Nature is only the occasion. The sublime is the mind's discovery that its reason and freedom exceed anything nature can overwhelm.

quiz.question: Kant's remark that the problem of setting up a state can be solved even for a nation of devils shows he believed peace required people to become saints first.
quiz.explanation: The opposite: Kant thought good institutions could make even selfish people behave as if they were good.

goDeeper.body:
Kant's short essay on enlightenment has an extraordinary afterlife. Two hundred years later, Michel Foucault (whom we meet on Day 81) wrote an essay with the same title, “What Is Enlightenment?” (1984). Foucault, often seen as a critic of Enlightenment reason, nonetheless praised Kant's essay for inventing a new kind of philosophical question: not “what is eternally true?” but “what is our present, and what are we doing in it?” He suggested that what we should inherit from the Enlightenment is not a set of doctrines but an attitude: a permanent critique of our own historical moment.

*Perpetual Peace* also became one of the most debated texts in international relations. In the 1980s the political scientist Michael Doyle drew on it to argue for what became known as the “democratic peace”: the empirical observation that established liberal democracies have rarely, if ever, fought wars against one another. The finding is contested — critics debate the definitions of “democracy” and “war”, and point out that democracies have often fought non-democracies and intervened covertly against elected governments. But Kant's idea that the internal structure of a state shapes its external behavior is now a mainstream hypothesis. The League of Nations (1920) and the United Nations (1945) are often described as distant descendants of his league of peace, though Kant would note that they lack his first condition: that every member be a republic.

In aesthetics, Kant's “disinterestedness” became a central and controversial idea. It underpinned the formalist theories of art of the early twentieth century, which judged paintings by form alone. Later critics, from Nietzsche to the sociologist Pierre Bourdieu in *Distinction* (1979), argued that the supposedly universal, disinterested taste Kant described is in fact the taste of a particular educated class.

questions: Is Kant's distinction between public and private uses of reason a defense of freedom or a compromise with power?
Can a judgment of taste really claim universal agreement, or is beauty ultimately in the eye of the beholder (or the social class)?
Does Kant's theory of the sublime explain why people seek out storms, mountains and even horror films?
